figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overview of D3D. (a) Drafter training. Target-generated responses supervise blockwise denoising and auxiliary autoregressive prediction. Packed attention shares causal prefix computation while isolating diffusion blocks and allowing bidirectional attention within each block. (b) Progressive layer pruning. Each iteration removes the layer causing the smallest decrease in validation acceptance length, followed by recovery and reevaluation of layer importance. Recovery uses distillation from a fixed unpruned drafter whose output distribution is adjusted toward the supervised token. (c) Asynchronous inference. During target verification, one packed drafter pass prepares successor blocks for alternative rejection outcomes and full acceptance. A branch matching the verified prefix is reused; otherwise, the drafter generates a new block synchronously.
figures.headline: The overview diagram shows training, layer pruning, and asynchronous inference in which one packed drafter pass prepares successor blocks.
citing_sentences: Figure 1 summarizes the training, pruning, and inference stages.
We pack the $K$ diffusion blocks into a single sequence to obtain denoising supervision for the masked positions following each anchor in one forward pass (Figure 1(a)).
With the target model and block size fixed, we measure validation acceptance length after separately removing each remaining layer (Figure 1(b)).

To test whether depth reduction improves speedup with little loss in acceptance, we evaluate progressively pruned and recovered D3D-8B checkpoints under asynchronous inference (Figure 2, left).

abstract: Target-conditioned diffusion drafters predict candidate tokens in parallel, yet each new block must wait for updated target-model hidden states. This forces drafting and verification to run sequentially, limiting speedup even though each block is generated in one pass. We introduce D3D, a standalone diffusion drafter that removes this inter-round dependency. D3D combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision to achieve long accepted prefixes without target hidden states. This independence lets D3D draft successor blocks during verification in one packed pass, enabling asynchronous speculative decoding. We progressively prune layers according to their effect on acceptance length to reduce the cost of packed drafting. Removing five of 36 layers retains over 99% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks with Qwen3-8B as the target. Across seven benchmarks, D3D averages 5.00$\times$ and 5.71$\times$ decoding speedup with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets, compared with 4.03$\times$ and 3.67$\times$ for DFlash. On GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, speedup reaches 7.48$\times$. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/fudan-generative-vision/D3D.

sections.body: Speculative decoding lets a draft model propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Parallel drafters such as DFlash condition on fresh target-model representations, so each new draft block waits for the previous verification round. D3D is a standalone diffusion drafter that does not use target hidden states. The introduction lists three contributions: target-aligned training, which at block size 16 gives a mean acceptance length of 7.88 with Qwen3-8B and 7.73 with Qwen3-32B; layer pruning; and asynchronous decoding, with mean speedups of 5.00× and 5.71× across seven benchmarks.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Target-conditioned drafters must wait for fresh target states, so drafting and verification run sequentially.

sections.body: Parallel drafters such as PARD, DFlash, and D2SD condition on target features, and PARD-2 can run with or without them. D3D shares target-independent inference with PARD and PARD-2, but learns its own prefix representations from diffusion and autoregressive supervision, with bidirectional attention inside masked blocks. For layer pruning, ShortGPT ranks layers by input-output similarity, and SDFP uses Fisher information without recovery training. D3D instead measures each layer's effect on acceptance length and alternates removal with recovery. For asynchronous decoding, SSD caches follow-up drafts for possible verification outcomes; D3D combines this idea with its own training and pruning.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior drafters mostly condition on target features, whereas D3D trains without them and prunes layers.

sections.body: Training uses target-generated responses. Masked blocks follow sampled anchor tokens and are denoised with exponentially decaying position weights, combined with an auxiliary next-token loss on unmasked responses. Pruning removes the layer whose removal lowers validation acceptance length the least, then runs recovery training with distillation from the fixed unpruned drafter, and reevaluates layer importance. At inference, one packed pass prepares blocks for each rejection outcome and for full acceptance, with asynchronous draft budget `N_async` = B[(C-1)F+2] for block size B, coverage C, and fan-out F. A cache hit hides drafting when packed drafting takes no longer than verification.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: D3D trains a standalone drafter, prunes layers by acceptance loss, and prepares successor blocks during verification.

sections.body: Experiments use Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets on seven math, code, and chat benchmarks, and compare against DFlash, DSpark, EAGLE-3, PARD-2, and SSD. Training prompts come from Open-PerfectBlend, which has 1.42 million examples, and responses are regenerated by the target in non-thinking mode. In the pruning ablation, reducing D3D-8B from 36 to 31 layers cuts depth by 13.9% and retains over 99% of mean τ, raising mean speedup from 4.44× to 4.69× across three benchmarks. Pretrained initialization reaches τ≈9.8 on GSM8K, versus τ≈4.5 for random initialization. On GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, speedup reaches 7.48×.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: D3D averages 5.00× and 5.71× decoding speedup, above DFlash's 4.03× and 3.67×, on seven benchmarks.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the training method, which combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision and uses no target hidden states. It also restates acceptance-guided pruning with recovery training. It reports average speedups of 5.00× and 5.71× over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets. The authors state that these averages exceed those of SSD and asynchronously deployed PARD-2 in their evaluation. Pruning from 36 to 31 layers retains over 99% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks. The section adds no new limitations.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The authors claim the first empirical demonstration of asynchronous lossless speculative decoding with a standalone diffusion drafter.

sections.body: The evaluation places the target on one GPU and the drafter on another, and the drafter adds model memory and speculative computation. The authors have not compared throughput per GPU against alternative uses of the same two GPUs, such as tensor-parallel target inference. A cache miss requires synchronous drafting before verification can resume. The implementation uses Transformers, and evaluation in production frameworks with batching and scheduling optimizations is left for future work.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Limitations are the extra drafter memory, synchronous drafting on cache misses, and no test in production serving frameworks.

sections.body: Appendix A gives the smallest mixing weight that makes the supervised token's margin at least delta, with delta set to 0.01. Appendix B finds that auxiliary weight 1 gives the highest GSM8K acceptance among tested weights. Block size 32 raises τ from 9.89 to 12.39 on MATH-500, but speedup falls from 5.55× to 3.16×, so block size 16 is kept. Going from 64 to 256 anchors adds at most 0.06 tokens on any task. Appendix C tests selective prefilling on LongBench with Qwen3-32B: with the 8B drafter at 10% retention, E2E speedup rises from 1.40× to 3.32× and the score is 47.05, versus 47.91 for the full prompt.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers the teacher-adjustment formula, extra ablations on training weight, block size and anchors, and selective prefilling on LongBench.
